work_order.approach:
Two files. One declaration in the stylesheet, and one abstraction in the test file that every stylesheet pin in it then uses, so that at the end of this change there is no second CSS parser left in the suite, plus the repair that makes the suite green so any of it can be verified. The diagnosis is settled and this round does not reopen it. What changes this round is four acceptance clauses the critique caught, one row the plan never specified, and one marker hazard the plan created.

R1 — ONE RULE ABOUT THE TERMINATING SEMICOLON, STATED ONCE. declarations(body, prop) treats a trailing chunk after the last ';' as a declaration, and every pin that reads through it therefore stays GREEN when a declaration loses its terminator. It is a STATED LOOSENING, stated in one place (AC-6(v)) and quoted nowhere except where a mutation is derived from it. M9 (the ';' off `.page-title`'s line-height: 1.25) and M10 (the ';' off `#main > *`'s min-width: 0) are both GREEN. What guards `#main > *`'s terminator afterwards is nothing, and out_of_scope says so in those words with the CSS rule that makes it correct — a declaration's terminating ';' is optional when it is the last one in a block, so `.page-title { margin: 0; line-height: 1.25 }` and the same rule with the semicolon are identical to every browser. A pin that reddens on the difference is a pin on punctuation rather than on the property it exists to protect, which is the defect class this ticket was filed about. The critique lists this as a regression risk because it applies to all twenty-four assertions rather than the two the plan names; that is the same fact, already stated, and the critique does not ask for it to be reversed.

R2 — `.page-title` READS THROUGH declarations(), AND CARRIES ITS NON-EMPTY GUARD ACROSS. Today the pin is a first-match `exec` plus `assert.ok(rule, 'src/web/styles.css defines a .page-title rule')` plus three `assert.match(rule[1], ...)` calls — first-match only, terminator-required. After this change it collects every NON-NESTED rule whose comma-split selector part is exactly `.page-title`, and that collection is asserted NON-EMPTY with the SAME message, before anything is asserted about its declarations. This clause is new and it is not optional: deleting the `.page-title` rule from a scratch copy reads 70 pass / 2 fail with the .page-title test red today, and that redness comes from the assert.ok. forEach over an empty collection is vacuously true, so a migration that drops the guard turns the suite GREEN on a stylesheet with no .page-title rule at all — a deleted rule, the exact inverse of a second rule being appended. The strictness that is a real gain is preserved and is what M13 covers: appending `.page-title { margin: 4rem; }` is green under first-match and breaks the page, and under the every-match form it is red.

R3 — THE SIX EXISTING PINS KEEP NESTED RULES IN THEIR MIGRATED COLLECTIONS. This is the correction that costs the most if an implementer gets it wrong. Today all six collect their rules with a global matchAll, which matches a rule wherever it sits, including inside an @media block. The coverage is live rather than theoretical, and it was measured on this tree rather than inherited: appending `@media (max-width: 900px) { .table-scroll { overflow-x: visible; } }` to src/web/styles.css makes `node --test test/web/pages.test.js` read 70 pass / 2 fail, the extra failure being the narrow-layout test, and the file was afterwards restored byte-identically. An implementer who applies the new pin's non-nested filter to the six as well — the natural reading of 'one reader, one rule' — silently deletes six live nested-override checks and the suite goes green on exactly the defect this ticket exists to close. So: the six keep EVERY rule, top-level or nested, that matches their selector; the non-nested filter belongs to the new .awaiting-list pin alone. M12 pins it and is the one row a single implementer command settles.

R4 — THE REPAIR FOR THE PRE-EXISTING RED USES THE FILE'S OWN IDIOM. Replace `/<li class="approval-card">/` with the token test the card pin already uses fifteen lines below it: extract the class attribute, split it on whitespace, assert the resulting Set contains approval-card, and separately assert the element carries `data-testid="approval-card"` per .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md. The regex `/<li\b[^>]*\bclass="[^"]*\bapproval-card\b[^"]*"/` is NOT used: `\b` after approval-card matches at a hyphen boundary, so it accepts `<li class="approval-card-extra">` and `<li class="not-approval-card">` where the form it replaces rejects both. That is a new false negative on the rename axis #71 finding 2 was filed about, in the file that documents the lesson, and the token form is immune to it while still matching the shipped markup.

R5 — THE `#main:focus` PAIR GETS A STATED COLLECTION POLICY EACH, because an earlier round mandated migrating these two pins and stated no policy for either, and the two candidate readings fail in opposite directions.

  The 345 pin collects every rule whose comma-split selector part is exactly `#main:focus` AND that is NOT nested, requires the collection NON-EMPTY, and asserts declarations(body, 'outline') deepEqual ['none'] on each. TOP LEVEL ONLY, and the reason is the file, not taste: the stylesheet has two such rules — one at top level with `outline: none` and one nested inside the `@media (forced-colors: active)` block with `outline: 2px solid CanvasText` — and the other test in the pair owns the second one at a different value. Collecting both and asserting none on each false-reds the shipped file, which is the one thing a migration must not do. A second TOP-LEVEL `#main:focus` rule is red here (M20), which is a verdict a first-match reader also misses.

  The 359 pin collects every NESTED rule whose selector part is exactly `#main:focus`, requires it non-empty, asserts declarations(body, 'outline') deepEqual ['2px solid CanvasText'] on EACH, and compares the two rules' SOURCE INDICES rather than the character offsets the file uses today. This is strictly stronger than the assertion it replaces and it is what closes the first-match blind spot: the pin today is a single non-global exec, so `@media (max-width: 900px) { #main:focus { outline: auto; } }` appended to the stylesheet is invisible to it and the suite stays green. Under R5 that mutation is red (M19). It keeps the length > 0 guard on the not-at-top-level lookup, so a reader regression that stopped descending into at-rules cannot make the test pass vacuously on a file with no carve-out at all, and it RE-SOURCES the `bareRuleAt !== -1` guard from the reader rather than leaving it on raw text, where it silently changes meaning once the comment strip is in play — the stylesheet mentions `#main:focus` in prose in the comment above the rule.

  One consequence to state because it moved: the forced-colors pin's OLD regex only found the carve-out when it was the first thing in the block, so the reader's rewrite is strictly MORE PERMISSIVE and M18 is GREEN on purpose. 'Another nested rule before the carve-out' now means a rule with a DIFFERENT selector — a second `#main:focus` rule in the block is RED under the per-rule value assertion, which is the correct verdict, and it is stated so the row cannot be read two ways.

R6 — THE DESCENDANT LIST IS A WATCH LIST, NOT AN ALLOW LIST, AND SAYS SO. AC-8(d) passes four selectors to conflictingOverrides, which reports any rule outside the pinned set declaring the property on any of them at any index. The consequence is that a CORRECT fix authored one level down — `.awaiting-list li span { overflow-wrap: anywhere; }`, the same inherited fix M6 accepts when it is placed on the parent — joins no collection and is reported as a conflict. That verdict is defensible: the pin is anchored on the li, the collection is the thing the fix must join, and a descendant-level declaration is a different edit from the one the stylesheet's own comment describes. What was not defensible was having neither a policy nor a matrix row for it, so the test's own comment now says the descendant entries are a WATCH list — a correct descendant-level fix is conservatively reported — and M6b names that verdict. Nothing is dropped from the list: dropping strong and span would turn the check into a same-selector check only, which is what the pin's own collection predicate already does.

R7 — THE MATRIX'S MARKERS ARE AN IDENTIFIER AND ARE CONSTRAINED; ITS PROSE IS NOT. (New this round, and neither the proposal nor the critique raised it.) The row format is `// <ROW-ID>  <RED|GREEN>  <free prose>`, the prose after the token is asserted about by nothing, and the new case finds the block as the text between its two marker comments. That leaves one unguarded edge: a row whose prose contains a marker string silently moves the block's boundaries, and the case that exists to catch a deleted block would then certify a truncated one. The fix costs nothing because it lands on strings this order already fixes — the two marker comments are chosen by the plan, so each occurs once in the file and no row's prose may contain either. This is the same reasoning as the H1_HOOK phrase constraint, with the sign flipped: there, unconstrained prose must not be allowed to decide a check; here, unconstrained prose must not be allowed to move one.

A. Add `overflow-wrap: anywhere;` to the EXISTING `.awaiting-list li` rule in src/web/styles.css, in place among its display / gap / border / border-radius / padding declarations, with a comment above the rule giving the wrap rule's reason the way the one above the four-card rule does. The comment is constrained by CONTENT and not by wording: it must give (a) that a grid item's automatic minimum is its min-content width, (b) anywhere rather than break-word, and (c) that the declaration reaches the strong by inheritance. It MAY or MAY NOT name the property in prose, and MUST NOT be written to any length. The plan previously constrained the comment's VOICE and then asserted a number the voice's wording decided; the two must not both happen, and every number in this order that depends on the comment's wording has been deleted rather than recomputed. No second rule with the same selector RE-DECLARES the property: the new pin collects every non-nested rule on that selector whose body declares the property and asserts the value on each, so such a rule joins the collection and reads RED against the VALUE assertion (M3a) — that is the mechanism, and it is NOT conflictingOverrides, which exempts the whole collected set by design and can never report a rule that joined it. A second rule on the same selector that leaves overflow-wrap alone is not collected and is GREEN (M3b), which is correct: a rule that neither declares overflow-wrap nor uses the all shorthand cannot change that property's computed value. The all bound is not decoration — `.awaiting-list li { all: revert; }` declares no overflow-wrap, so the collection and the conflict helper both skip it, and all resets the property to its initial value and reinstates the overflow with a green suite. The stylesheet already uses a `*` rule, so the shorthand is in house style. The bound is recorded in out_of_scope rather than pinned.

B. Add four shared helpers near the top of test/web/pages.test.js, beside H1_HOOK and mainOf, and route all eight stylesheet read sites through them.

  readStylesheet() — the single readFileSync of src/web/styles.css, returning the SOURCE STRING. Every one of the eight sites becomes `const css = readStylesheet();`, the shape they have today, and the parse is one call on top. Its call KEEPS the `readFileSync(new URL('../../src/web/styles.css', import.meta.url), 'utf8')` form all eight sites have today, which is part of the helper's pinned shape: AC-4 is a shape check about which readFileSync occurrences survive, and that form is what makes this one identifiable. It returns the string rather than the parsed rules on purpose: the non-empty guards and failure messages in those eight tests are about the FILE. Line 1611's readFileSync is NOT migrated: it reads test/web/pages.test.js itself inside the H1_HOOK call-site pin.

  cssRules(source) — strip /* */ with the SAME expression the card pin uses today, then walk with a brace stack. A frame whose selector starts with '@' is a BLOCK whose children are rules; any other frame is a rule whose body is declarations. ';' terminates a declaration inside a rule and a prelude inside an at-rule. Nested rules are emitted with their own selector and a nested flag meaning 'not at top level'. At-rule frames are not emitted. Every rule carries a source index. ONE EXCEPTION, and it is in the shipped file today: a block whose prelude is @keyframes (or @-webkit-keyframes) contains KEYFRAME STEPS, not style rules — skip its children entirely rather than emitting 0% / 100% as rules. A 0% selector matches nothing on a comma-split === comparison, so the mis-emission is harmless to every pin today, but it puts junk into the one structure every other helper depends on. TWO OTHER FAILURE MODES PRODUCE PLAUSIBLE OUTPUT AND NEITHER SHOWS UP UNTIL A PIN DEPENDS ON IT: accumulating the prelude through a rule body concatenates the last declaration onto the selector of the next nested rule (M16), and a reader that appends nested text to the parent body instead of descending into it drops every nested rule and reinstates the at-rule blind spot exactly (M11) — M11 is green under that second bug while every test in the file as written today still passes. This order pins NO rule count: a total breaks on every future stylesheet edit for no semantic reason and would not have caught either.

  declarations(body, prop) — one property's values from an already comment-stripped body, anchored on a declaration boundary (start of body, or after a ';') rather than a bare substring, with a trailing chunk after the last ';' treated as a declaration. THE REASONS FOR THE ANCHORING ARE MEASURED, and one commonly cited reason is false: 'min-width' is NOT a substring of 'min-height'. The reasons that are real, both green today: (a) a rule with no min-width at all but a comment naming one reads as a single value and the pin passes — the BUG-1 state passing the BUG-1 pin, because the min-width pin does not strip comments while the card pin beside it does; (b) a comment standing beside a real declaration is consumed as the declaration, so the widths come back as two values where the real floor is one. The third thing the boundary buys is the custom-property case: a bare substring search matches `--min-width: 16ch` and a boundary-anchored one does not, in a stylesheet whose :root declares seventeen custom properties. The trailing-chunk clause is R1 and nothing else.

  conflictingOverrides(rules, pinned, selectors, prop) — the card pin's override loop, lifted out of that test's body and corrected. The property is a fourth argument and the filter `declarations(other.body, prop).length > 0` runs INSIDE, because the card pin's existing /overflow-wrap\s*:/ filter is what makes the comment above it true — a rule that cannot override the card classes does not turn the suite red. Take the property away and you get one of two failures: drop the filter and a narrow-viewport padding tweak on a pinned selector turns the suite red for a declaration that cannot change the property, re-breaking a tolerance #71 added on purpose; or hardcode overflow-wrap inside and the non-wrap pins get a check that can never fire. pinned is the rule or the SET of rules the calling pin has already asserted on, and every member is exempt — without the exemption the fix itself would be reported as an override of itself. A conflict is reported for any rule other than the pinned set, at ANY source index, top-level or nested, declaring prop on a comma-split selector part equal to a member of selectors. Symmetric in source order, because an override authored above the pinned rule wins at narrow viewports exactly as one below does. The nested half is the fix for review finding 3 and is M4.

  THE SELECTOR LOOKUP MUST ANCHOR ON THE SELECTOR'S END — compare a comma-split part to the pinned selector with ===, never `selector.includes(pinnedSelector)`. '.opportunity-roww' and '.tenant-names' both contain their pinned selector as a substring; the current `\s*\{` anchors give the pins their rename protection today, and a substring lookup deletes it across all eight pins at once, invisibly. M14 is the GREEN that proves it survives.

  WHERE THE CONFLICT CHECK IS CALLED, and this is the design decision that matters most. Call it at the card pin and at the new .awaiting-list pin ONLY. The `#main > *`, `.table-scroll`, `.approval-actions`, `.approval-actions input`, `.journal-drawer-body` and `.tenant-name` pins each already collect EVERY rule matching their selector — top-level and nested, per R3 — and assert the property on every one of them, so their every-match loop IS that selector's override check, and it is stronger than a same-selector conflict check because it also catches a rule declaring the WRONG value. Because the helper exempts the pinned set, and on those six the pinned set is every rule that could ever match, a call there could never fire: dead code that reads as coverage. Put one comment line in each of those six tests saying the every-match loop is that selector's override check, so the absence reads as a decision. The distinction is pinned by contract case C10 so it cannot rot silently.

  THE CARD PIN KEEPS ITS OWN PRE-FILTER — the one place a migration could false-red on a correct stylesheet. Today the card pin builds its candidate set, filters it with `/overflow-wrap\s*:/.test(rule.body)`, and only then calls .find(). That filter is load-bearing: without it find() returns the border / padding / display rule carrying two of the four card classes, with no overflow-wrap at all, and both the selector-set equality assertion and the deepEqual(values, ['anywhere']) assertion go RED on the shipped file. This pre-filter is DISTINCT from the one inside conflictingOverrides, and both survive the migration. It is named in AC-6 so nobody simplifies it away.

  THE NEW `.awaiting-list` PIN, in the house style of `#main > *` and `.tenant-name` rather than a whole-body assertion, and in ONE test. In order: (a) collect every rule that is NOT nested, whose comma-split selector part is `.awaiting-list` or `.awaiting-list li`, and whose body DECLARES overflow-wrap — the property filter is part of the COLLECTION predicate, not only inside the helper, and the test's own comment must say that in those terms, because a rule added at M5 inside a media query has a selector part that IS exactly `.awaiting-list li` and an unfiltered collection takes it in, at which point the value assertion fails and the suite goes red for a fix that was never the defect; (b) require the collection NON-EMPTY, with a message that says so, so deleting the declaration and leaving a comment is red (M1), and today's `.awaiting-list li` rule has zero overflow-wrap declarations in it, so (b) is what turns the current state red rather than vacuous; (c) require each collected rule's overflow-wrap values to deepEqual ['anywhere'] (M2 is this clause's row, and it is specified here because the matrix enumerated it without defining it); (d) run conflictingOverrides(rules, collected, four selectors, 'overflow-wrap') and require it to report nothing, under R6's watch-list policy. IT DOES NOT READ `display`, and that is a decision with four parts agreeing on it — out_of_scope declines to police display, the pin's five clauses never mention it, qa_script step 5(iii) demonstrates `display: flex` staying green as a finding, and residual_risks names it. AC-1 no longer asks it to. TWO STRICTNESSES WITH THEIR COSTS RECORDED. First, the descendant entries in (d) are a snapshot of the awaiting li's element children — the markup was rendered rather than assumed, and it emits exactly `<strong>` and one `<span>`, with no other element child — and they are not an exhaustive set: a third element child carrying free text is invisible to the conflict check with a green suite, which is the descendant hole (M7, M8) in the list rather than in the descendant. Second, the collection requires the declaration at TOP LEVEL, because a fix authored only inside `@media (max-width: 900px)` satisfies the new pin in full AND satisfies the whole browser sweep at 320 / 375 / 414, all of which are inside that query, while the defect is not inherently narrow-viewport (M5, RED on purpose).

C. THE MUTATION MATRIX, INSERTED AS A COMMENT BLOCK AT THE END of test/web/pages.test.js, one row per line in the fixed shape `// <ROW-ID>  <RED|GREEN>  <free prose>`, between two marker comments, with the prose after the verdict token unconstrained and asserted about by nothing, and with the two markers constrained per R7. A matrix that lives only in a plan document is deleted with the plan and enforces nothing, which is why it is inserted here; the cost of inserting it is one self-referential constraint — the H1_HOOK call-site pin reads this file as its own source — which is why AC-13 states its shape check with no count and no line number, and why the row format fixes an identifier and a verdict token and nothing else. work_order.confidence_rationale:
The root cause is the one part I can vouch for from the tree rather than from a document: I read the two rules, read the markup that renders into them, and ran the suite (72 tests, 71 pass, 1 fail, the failure being the pre-existing matcher this order repairs). The product fix is one declaration whose mechanism is CSS inheritance, confirmed by the stylesheet's own comment above the four-card rule that works the same way, and no criterion depends on a pixel. I also re-ran the critique's four load-bearing claims rather than accepting either document's account, and all four reproduced: the eleven assertion messages that make AC-4 unsatisfiable, the four truthiness guards that make AC-12 a misdescription, the display:grid contradiction between AC-1 and four other statements, and the two bare enumerations that are M2's only mentions. The corrections above are small, local and each one I can point at the line that made it necessary.

What holds this at 68 rather than in the eighties is not the design, it is the second half of the change. Twenty-four of the twenty-five matrix verdicts have never been executed, because the four helpers they exercise do not exist yet; R5's two collection policies make two shipped pins stricter than they are today with nothing run against either; R2's non-empty guard is a clause a person can drop without any test noticing; and R7's marker constraint is new this round and, by construction, cannot catch a test that locates the block the same wrong way the block was written. The critique's own verdict is that the design is right and the acceptance layer is not — and the acceptance layer has now been wrong in three consecutive rounds, once per round, each time in a way only a careful reader found. A pattern that regular is evidence about everything else the document asserts, which is exactly what a confidence score is for. What would raise it: M12 run against the migrated tree, or any three of the matrix rows run at all, or a browser driver so AC-2 stops depending on figures nobody can reproduce here. What would lower it: an implementer reporting M12 green after the migration, which would mean six live checks were retired, or a fourth acceptance defect of this class found by a reader. I am below the gate on purpose. The design is not the reason to stop this plan; the unexecuted migration is, and a person reading residual_risks and the matrix is the cheapest way to settle that.
work_order.debate_summary:
The critique returned 'flawed' with seven findings against v15 — one blocking, three major, three minor — plus five regression risks. It is right about the diagnosis, right about the design, and right about all four findings I re-ran. I upheld the blocking finding and all three majors, took two minors in a lighter form than filed, and rejected the rest with reasons below. The disagreement that survives is the one that has survived four rounds, and the round's other significant event is that I found one hazard neither document had.

THE BLOCKING FINDING IS A REAL CONTRADICTION, AND THE OBVIOUS FIX IS THE WRONG ONE. AC-1 required the new pin to assert `display: grid`; out_of_scope[1], AC-8, qa_script step 5(iii) and residual_risks[1] each require the pin to stay silent on that property, and step 5(iii) requires the `display: flex` mutation to stay GREEN. I checked the pin's clauses and the string 'display' is in none of them. The critique offers no fix, only the contradiction, which is the right shape for a finding this clean. I resolved it by deleting the assertion from AC-1 rather than by adding it to the pin, and this is the one place I disagree with the obvious reading: making AC-1 assertable means policing `display`, which out_of_scope declines on stated grounds, which turns a mutation qa_script deliberately demonstrates into a failure, and which is precisely the shape of the objection the last rejection raised — a criterion no machine can run. AC-1 now says what CI settles and says out loud that the location clause is a requirement on the diff, and residual_risks names it as the one acceptance claim in the order that no CI case settles, so the gap is visible to a reviewer instead of buried in a contradiction.

THE THREE MAJORS WERE ALL REAL AND ALL ARE FIXED, AND ONE OF THEM IS THE BRIEF'S OWN OBJECTION HALF-ANSWERED. AC-4's counts were deleted in v15 and the shape check that replaced them was also false: 'no other line names src/web/styles.css' cannot hold while AC-12 preserves eleven assertion messages that name it. I ran the grep — 19 lines, eight reads and eleven messages — so the review's second objection and the critique's first major are the same defect seen from two sides, and deleting the numbers was not sufficient. AC-4's scope is now the CALL, its verifier greps the `readFileSync(new URL` form rather than the bare identifier, and it says outright that the eleven messages are required to survive. M2 was enumerated by AC-5 and by qa_script step 6 and defined nowhere; that is a hole in a matrix whose completeness a new CI case enforces, so the test would have certified whatever an implementer invented, and the critique is right that no other check in the order can tell a row that was never written from one that was. I specified it: the wrong-value mutation, `anywhere` to `break-word`, which is the only clause of the new pin that otherwise had no row. AC-12 claimed a `length > 0` guard on all eight sites when four use assert.ok on a single match, and its verifier described an assertion on the stylesheet TEXT that no site makes and this order does not add. Confirmed by reading all eight. AC-12 now states both forms, says which three tests gain an explicit collection assertion from R2 and R5, and keeps the under-matching-is-safe argument, which holds for either shape — that argument is what residual_risks leans on, so misdescribing its mechanism mattered more than the finding's size suggests.

TWO MINORS TAKEN IN A LIGHTER FORM, ONE DISMISSED. The H1_HOOK hazard is real and the critique understates it: the matrix block goes in at the END of the file, so a marker in its prose cannot re-point a `find` that resolves the first hit, but the HELPER block goes in above line 216 and can. AC-13 now constrains every line this order adds, at any position. The fixture-choice finding is taken at its smallest: the critique itself calls the substitution benign, so AC-8(e) now says the wrapper is immaterial rather than mandating one. DISMISSED: the critique's third minor — that AC-6(vi)'s ch-only narrowing has no matrix row id, so the one constraint in AC-6 that changes what a shipped test accepts is uncheckable. The observation is correct and I acted on it, but by ADDING the row rather than by dropping the constraint: M22, `min-width: 16ch` to `12px`, RED under the narrowing and GREEN on the unmodified tree. The critique offers narrowing-versus-row as if the constraint had to go; it does not. A declared narrowing with a row that demonstrates exactly what it costs is stronger than an unremarked one, and the row is what makes the future redness someone will hit legible rather than surprising.

WHAT I FOUND THAT NEITHER DOCUMENT HAD. The new case that keeps the matrix alive finds the block as the text between its two marker comments; the row format constrains the identifier and the verdict token and explicitly leaves the prose free, asserted about by nothing. So a row whose prose contains a marker string silently moves the block's boundaries, and the case that exists to catch a deleted block would certify a truncated one. It is the same species as the H1_HOOK constraint with the sign flipped: there, unconstrained prose must not be allowed to decide a check; here, it must not be allowed to move one. R7 closes it on strings this order already fixes, so it costs nothing, and risks says what it cannot catch: a test that locates the block the same wrong way the block was written.

WHAT I REJECTED, AND WHY. The critique's scope paragraph — that the extraction remains large for a one-declaration fix — is the fourth round it has raised, and I reject the split again. The issue's own review called the extraction 'Optional, and not worth blocking on' while taking its own advice on each of the four findings it filed, so 'optional' was about the extraction as a vehicle for findings that were not optional. A split puts one line of CSS in a different ticket from the parser that pins it, which is how the false 'measured and safe' memory entry that started this chain was written. I am not going to answer that real risk by making the plan smaller. Three of the critique's five regression risks I also treat as restatements rather than findings: R1 as a global loosening, the ch-only narrowing's future cost, and M3b's uncollected-rule tolerance are each already a declared decision carried in out_of_scope, risks and assumptions, and I have kept all three visible there while noting the first is a real cost in out_of_scope's own words. The two that are findings rather than restatements — the display:grid contradiction and the marker hazard — are fixed above.

CONFIDENCE IS BELOW THE GATE, DELIBERATELY. 68, against a min_confidence of 70, and the arbiter instruction not to inflate the number is the whole point of the instrument: four of the last six rounds of this plan were rejected for a number or a label that was wrong, and this round the critique found a blocking acceptance contradiction and three majors in a plan that had just been rewritten to fix two acceptance findings. The product fix is not in doubt. The unexecuted migration is, and the cheapest way to settle it is a person running the matrix — M12 first, since it is the one row that needs no helper — which is why tests[] puts the matrix first, why qa_script step 6 names the twenty-five-run budget, and why residual_risks leads with the fact that the layout defect itself has no automated coverage at all. I would rather hand this to a person who can run twenty-five mutations than ship a number that says the risk was considered. The issue carries no `## Acceptance (from the split)` section, which I confirmed against both the issue body and brief.md, so there is no IAC-n to satisfy or defer by number and every deferral is named in out_of_scope in words.
